analysis.one_liner: Caps prices and opens licenses for COVID-19 drugs developed with federal funding.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees in June 2020, none of which took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any COVID-19 drug, treatment, or vaccine developed in whole or in part with federal funding to be sold at a fair and reasonable price, and would bar exclusive monopolies on those inventions: if a company received federal support, the government could grant open, nonexclusive licenses letting other manufacturers make the drug, with the original patent holder paid a reasonable royalty. It would also let the Health and Human Services Secretary void a drug's FDA marketing exclusivity and license other manufacturers if the price during a public health emergency was found excessive. Finally, it would require drugmakers to publicly report their development costs, federal funding received, and pricing decisions, with fines for missing or false reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who need COVID-19 treatments and vaccines, especially people who are uninsured or facing high out-of-pocket costs; taxpayer-funded health programs whose budgets are strained by drug prices; and potential generic and competing manufacturers who could make licensed versions. The bill's pricing test specifically weighs racial and socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 cases and deaths.

how_it_helps.text: Any company developing a COVID-19 drug with federal support must include fair-and-reasonable pricing terms in its contract, judged partly by the drug's impact on access and on racial and socioeconomic disparities in COVID-19 outcomes.

Federal licenses on federally funded COVID-19 inventions must be open and nonexclusive, so more than one manufacturer can make the drug; licensees pay the patent holder a reasonable royalty rather than nothing.

If HHS finds the price of a drug tied to a public health emergency is excessive, it can void the drug's FDA marketing exclusivity and license any manufacturer to produce it, with royalties paid to the original patent or exclusivity holder.

Manufacturers of COVID-19 drugs must publicly report what the drug cost to develop, how much came from federal funds, and their pricing decisions, with penalties of up to $100,000 per day for failing to report or per false item.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug and vaccine developers whose products relied on federal funding: they would lose sole rights to their inventions, face a price ceiling, and in extreme cases lose FDA exclusivity, in exchange for royalties set by the Secretary.

drawbacks.text: Forcing open licenses and price ceilings on any federally touched COVID-19 invention could reduce companies' incentive to invest in pandemic drug and vaccine development, or to partner with the government at all, since the payoff of exclusivity would shrink. [S3]

The bill gives the HHS Secretary broad, largely standardless discretion to decide what price is 'excessive' and what royalty is 'reasonable', which could invite inconsistent or politically driven determinations. [S3]

The measure reaches any invention a company developed 'in whole or in part' with federal support, however small that federal contribution, sweeping in privately funded products alongside genuinely government-backed ones. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: During a once-in-a-century pandemic, with taxpayer dollars flowing into vaccine and drug development, the public benefit of guaranteed affordable access and transparency about public investment is substantial, and the bill pays inventors royalties rather than expropriating them. The strongest honest objection is the innovation trade-off: open licensing and a government-set price ceiling could blunt the incentive to develop the very products a pandemic response needs, though the bill's royalty floor and its limits to emergencies and federally supported drugs are designed to soften that risk.

outcome.mechanism: The House sent the bill to four committees in June 2020; no committee held a markup or brought it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 22, 2020 by Rep. Janice Schakowsky with 34 cosponsors, including one Republican.
The same day, it was referred to four committees: Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, Science, Space and Technology, and Armed Services.
The action history records no further action by any committee, no markup, no floor vote, and the 116th Congress ended January 3, 2021 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patent-holding drug and vaccine developers that received federal funding kept exclusive control over their COVID-19 inventions and their pricing, with no competing licensed versions and no reporting of federal subsidies or pricing decisions. Patients bore whatever prices the market produced.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 33 Democratic and 1 Republican cosponsors.

for.name: 1 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican support.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the referral without a markup or floor recommendation for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary, Science, Space and Technology, and Armed Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the portions of the bill within their jurisdictions.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Fought against price-control and license-breaking measures on COVID-19 drugs during 2020, arguing they would undercut innovation incentives.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic (33 of the 34 cosponsors), with a single Republican cosponsor, and the bill never reached a floor vote that could have revealed a broader partisan split.

industries.industry: Brand-name pharmaceutical and vaccine makers with federal contracts
industries.note: The bill would cap their prices on federally supported COVID-19 drugs, strip exclusivity from overpriced ones, and open their patents to competing manufacturers in exchange for royalties. Their interest in keeping monopoly pricing ran against patients' interest in affordable access.
Open, nonexclusive licenses would let them manufacture and sell versions of federally funded COVID-19 drugs, expanding their market. Cheaper competing supply is also what lowers prices for patients.

industries.industry: Biotech startups dependent on federal R&D partnerships
industries.note: Universities and small developers that license federally funded inventions exclusively would lose the exclusivity that attracts private investment, since the government must grant open licenses instead.
